newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Battle for Belgian central bank board appears over.
newsitem.headline: Battle for Belgian central bank board appears over.

text.p: A battle for control of Belgium's central bank board was played out on Tuesday, paving the way for new statutes and a controversial gold coin sale plan to be adopted in parliament on Thursday.

Parliament's finance committee backed a government proposal to leave open the question of how large the bank's board should be once European economic and monetary union (EMU) starts, rejecting opposition demands the number of directors be reduced.

However, the battle left some ruling coalition party members embarrassed while opponents warned it could damage Belgium's chances of passing the independent central bank test -- one of the criteria for countries wishing to participate in EMU.
The draft law is itself designed to bring Belgium's central bank into compliance with the Maastricht Treaty.

"I am a member of the (governing) majority, but I think this decision is totally in contradiction with the spirit of the Maastricht Treaty, which I signed, giving independence to central banks," former Belgian foreign minister Mark Eyskens told Reuters after the meeting.

Opposition members were more scathing. Monetary economist Paul De Grauwe, a member of the Flemish liberal party, said the government's attempt not to say how many members would be on the board smacked of political opportunism.
"If politicians can just do this it raises issues about the independence of the central bank," De Grauwe said.

Belgium's central bank board is presently composed of six directors plus governor Alfons Verplaetse. Each effectively represents a major political party, with the two largest parties -- the Flemish christian democrats (CVP) and francophone socialists (PS) -- each having two seats.

Under the government amendment adopted on Tuesday, and which is almost certain now to be approved by the full parliament on Thursday, the board could be composed of between five and seven members plus the governor. At present its statutes state it should be between three and six plus the governor.

Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told the committee the enlargement could be needed because recent indications from the European Monetary Institute (EMI) were that the future European Central Bank would operate a decentralised monetary policy.

De Grauwe, Eyskens and others said, however, EMU would necessarily mean less work for the National Bank of Belgium, noting the Dutch and German central banks had decided to cut the size of their boards.

The real reason for the move, they said, was that the ruling CVP party of Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene could not decide how many members it wanted on the board once its two existing representatives, including Verplaetse, retire in 1999.

"The intention seems to me not to reduce numbers but to sort out a problem in the CVP," Walloon liberal Didier Reynders said, noting newspaper reports that Verplaetse and Dehaene appeared unable to agree on who should represent the party at the bank.
